newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African investors urged to focus on local bonds.
newsitem.headline: S.African investors urged to focus on local bonds.

text.p: The prospect of lower interest rates next year indicated investors should reduce their exposure to offshore investments and shares and set their sights on local bonds, Citadel Investment Services director Wikus Marais said.
Addressing an investment briefing on Wednesday, Marais also said he expected the rand to bottom out within the next six months and then strengthen.
He said many South Africans were worried about the economy for no proper reason as it should be judged against economic cycles rather than political events.
Although the economy had entered a downward phase, government remained committed to fiscal discipline and in the long term, the country was on the road to higher growth.

Marais said the rand's slide had been necessary because it had become overvalued on the back of higher inflows of foreign capital, rapid domestic money creation and the abolition of the financial rand.
Several factors, including the return to a current account surplus, indicated that it would bottom out in about six months and then strengthen in 1997.
Investment decisions, too, should be influenced by economic not political factors, Marais said.
For example, because the bulk of the rand's depreciation was now over, investors should start reducing their foreign exposure through asset swaps.
Another factor to bear in mind was that foreign assets were mostly invested in the U.S., which seemed set for a major correction.
With an interest rate cut due in South Africa next year, Marais said investors should start moving into fixed interest government stock instead while minimising exposure to domestic shares.

Commenting on calls for the removal of exchange controls, Marais said he expected their abolition to take time because there were no guarantees that anticipated outflows would be matched by foreign investment in South Africa.
"We know that there will be at least 100 billion rand of pension funds and institutional money wanting to leave the country just because of normal portfolio diversification," he said.
Given the lack of any guarantee that this would be matched by a compensating inflow of foreign money into the country, he felt the removal of exchange controls would take a while.
